messages.author: ca51dc784e0edba6
messages.subject: binomial-binomial model with stan
parts:
Hi all,

   I just wrote a binomial-binomial model using stan via brute-force marginalization. I think this would be a good example for those who want to marginalize discrete variables, so I post it here.

In BUGS notation, the following stan code is equivalent to 

model
{
   theta1 ~ dunif(0,1)
   theta2 ~ dunif(0,1)
   x ~ dbin(theta1,50)
   y ~ dbin(theta2,x)
}
DATA
list(
y = 5
)

In stan:

transformed data
{
   int y;
   int N;
   int K;
   y <- 5;
   N <- 50;
   K <- N-y+1;
}
parameters
{
   real<lower=0,upper=1> theta1;
   real<lower=0,upper=1> theta2;
}
model
{
   
   {
      real tmp_vec[K];
      for(k in y:N)
      {
         real tmp_factorial; #some terms are redundant, but I leave it for those who how I derive this 
         tmp_factorial <- (tgamma(N+1.0) /tgamma(k+1.0) / tgamma(N-k+1.0)) * (tgamma(k+1.0)/ tgamma(y+1.0) / tgamma(k-y+1.0));
         tmp_vec[k-y+1] <- tmp_factorial * pow(theta1,k) *pow(1.0-theta1,(N-k)) * pow(theta2,y)  * pow(1.0-theta2,(k-y));
      }
      increment_log_prob(log(sum(tmp_vec)));
   }
}

Enjoy!

messages.author: ca51dc784e0edba6
messages.subject: Re: binomial-binomial model with stan
parts:
I just made it via user defined function block.

functions
{
   void binbin_lp(int y_,int N_,real theta1_,real theta2_)
   {
      int K_;

      K_ <- N_ - y_ + 1;
      {
      real tmp_vec[K_];

      for(k_ in y_:N_)
      {
         real tmp_factorial;
         tmp_factorial <- (tgamma(N_+1.0) /tgamma(k_+1.0) / tgamma(N_-k_+1.0)) * (tgamma(k_+1.0)/ tgamma(y_+1.0) / tgamma(k_-y_+1.0));
         tmp_vec[k_-y_+1] <- tmp_factorial * pow(theta1_,k_) *pow(1.0-theta1_,(N_-k_)) * pow(theta2_,y_)  * pow(1.0-theta2_,(k_-y_));
      }
      increment_log_prob(log(sum(tmp_vec)));
      }
      return;
   }
}

Now, you can use binbin_jp in model block (in the manual, _lp signature is used for transformed parameters block, but we can use it in model block, too).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] binomial-binomial model with stan
parts:
Thanks for sharing. It's the same kind of thing
we'd have to do for binomial missing data. Was there
an application driving this?

I would think this would all be more arithmetically
stable on the log scale (less chance of underflow).
So my knee-jerk reaction is to convert the linear scale
formulation

> {

> real tmp_vec[K];
> for(k in y:N)
> {
> real tmp_factorial; #some terms are redundant, but I leave it for those who how I derive this
> tmp_factorial <- (tgamma(N+1.0) /tgamma(k+1.0) / tgamma(N-k+1.0)) * (tgamma(k+1.0)/ tgamma(y+1.0) / tgamma(k-y+1.0));
> tmp_vec[k-y+1] <- tmp_factorial * pow(theta1,k) *pow(1.0-theta1,(N-k)) * pow(theta2,y) * pow(1.0-theta2,(k-y));
> }
> increment_log_prob(log(sum(tmp_vec)));
> }

into the following log-scale version (which won't underflow or overflow
like the tgamma andprod are prone to do with large k or N, especially
wen multiplied together):

{
real log_tmp_vec[K];
for (k in y:N)
log_tmp_vec[k - y + 1]
<- lgamma(N + 1)
- lgamma(k + 1)
- lgamma(N - k + 1)
+ lgamma(k + 1)
- lgamma(y + 1)
- lgamma(k - y + 1)
+ k * log(theta1)
+ (N - k) * log1m(theta1)
+ y * log(theta2)
+ (k - y) * logm(theta2);
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log_tmp_vec));
}

But now I see the structure is just two binomials,
so I'm pretty sure everything reduces to this:

{
real tmp[K];
for (k in y:N)
tmp[k - y + 1]
<- binomial_log(k, N, theta1)
+ binomial_log(y, k, theta2);
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(tmp));
}

At least I think that'll give you the same model. It makes
sense given the original BUGS formulation, too.

And speaking of arithmetic, it's usually better to just work
on the int scale (both faster and more accurate) rather than forcing
early double conversion. That is, (k + 1) will evaluate the addition as
integers, then convert to double as the argument to lgamma. But doing
(k + 1.0) will first cast k to a double, then do the addition.

- Bob

On Jul 15, 2014, at 1:56 AM, Soga Shota <soga....@gmail.com> wrote:

> I just made it via user defined function block.

> functions
> {
> void binbin_lp(int y_,int N_,real theta1_,real theta2_)
> {
> int K_;
>
> K_ <- N_ - y_ + 1;
> {
> real tmp_vec[K_];
>

> {
> real tmp_factorial;
> tmp_factorial <- (tgamma(N_+1.0) /tgamma(k_+1.0) / tgamma(N_-k_+1.0)) * (tgamma(k_+1.0)/ tgamma(y_+1.0) / tgamma(k_-y_+1.0));
> tmp_vec[k_-y_+1] <- tmp_factorial * pow(theta1_,k_) *pow(1.0-theta1_,(N_-k_)) * pow(theta2_,y_) * pow(1.0-theta2_,(k_-y_));
> }
> increment_log_prob(log(sum(tmp_vec)));
> }
> return;
> }

If you define instead (and I'd suggest not using trailing underscores
for arguments --- those are conventionally used for member variables
in classes, at least in C++):

real binbin_log(int y, int N, real theta1, real theta2) {
... as in your code ...
return log(sum(tmp_vec));
}

The "_log" suffix is important --- it's what lets you call it as:

y ~ binbin(N, theta1, theta2);

in the model block. You can also use binbin_log() as a function,
and just wrap it in increment_log_prob() externally.

It's a very clunky name-mangling and identifier-based syntax
we're using --- very old-school Fortran.

- Bob

The important feature of log_sum_exp is that it won't overflow with
the exp() operation in either values or derivatives. It also has
analytic derivatives so it's faster than calling log(sum(exp(vec)))

I was thinking there might be such a reduction.

I can see that binomial(N, theta1 * theta2) will have
the same mean, but will it have the same variance? I
would think the compound version would be overdispersed,
but I don't know how to work out its variance other than
by simulation.

Presumably in the richer model, these won't be simple
parameters but the results of regressions on a log-odds
scale.

- Bob

I've experimented with binomial-binomial models in a setting where observations can be misclassified, so there are unobserved true values and observed values that are a function of the true values and the specificity (% true negative detected) and sensitivity (% true positive detected) of some test that determines positiveness. Because there are many sums of false and true positives that can lead to the observed values (and sums of true and false negatives that can lead to observed negatives), it is significantly more complicated to marginalize over all possible combinations, but the concept of marginalizing over all possible sums is similar to the current example (I think). Anyway, I found that a stan model based on marginalization behaved exactly the same as a simple model with: y ~ binomial(N, p_true * sensitivity + (1-p_true) * (1-specificity), including the uncertainty estimates.
